ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Pulmonology Consultation — John Locke — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two-week review of lung function and blood tests, diagnosis, start of treatment, and pulmonology consultation

text.paragraph: A 59-year-old never-smoker with a cough since his late thirties and wheeze and breathlessness, worse every winter, in city air, and by open coal and wood fires at home. Please confirm the diagnosis (asthma, COPD from non-tobacco exposures, or both), advise on CT, and recommend treatment and pulmonary rehabilitation. [S]
Urgency: Routine, within two to three weeks; he is not in distress and has a reliever. [S]

list.item: Does he have asthma, COPD from non-tobacco exposures, or features of both, and how should the airflow limitation be interpreted?
Is a CT of the chest indicated, and what does it show?
What treatment do you recommend?
Should he have pulmonary rehabilitation?
How much do outdoor air pollution and indoor solid-fuel smoke contribute, and what exposure reduction do you advise?
What monitoring and follow-up do you advise?

text.paragraph: Mr. Locke is seen at the request of Dr. Hartwell-Osei. He has had a cough since his late thirties, with wheeze and breathlessness that have grown over the years; symptoms are worst in winter, in cold air, in the city, and by smoky fires, and ease in summer and in the country. He has never smoked or vaped and has had no occupational dust or fume exposure. He lived about 30 years in a large city near main roads and for the past year has lodged in a country house with open coal and wood fires, which have been out of use for two weeks. He has had no hemoptysis, fevers, night sweats, weight loss, nasal symptoms, reflux, or breathlessness lying flat. He has never had an oral corticosteroid course or an emergency visit for breathing. On albuterol as needed he uses one or two doses a day. His father and brother died of consumption. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: John Locke was born on 29 August 1632 (Julian; 8 September 1632, Gregorian) at Wrington, Somerset, to Puritan parents of modest means. His father, John Locke (1606 to 1661), was a country attorney who served in a cavalry company on the Parliamentary side early in the Civil War; his mother was Agnes Keene. He had one brother, Thomas, born in 1637. [D]
He was educated at Westminster School and at Christ Church, Oxford, where he was elected to a studentship in 1652 and took his BA in 1656. [D]

His father died on 13 February 1660/1 (Julian), at about 54, of consumption or some kindred malady, by his biographer's account; his only brother, Thomas, died of consumption soon afterwards, at about 26, leaving no children. [D]

He studied medicine at Oxford and took the degree of Bachelor of Medicine in February 1674/5, with a licence to practise, but never took the doctorate. From 1667 he lived in the household of Lord Ashley (later the first Earl of Shaftesbury) as his physician, and in June 1668 he organized the surgical drainage of a large abscess above Ashley's liver, with advice from leading physicians including Thomas Sydenham. [D]

From about 1667 he was a close friend of the physician Thomas Sydenham, accompanied him on visits to patients, helped him with his writings, and was praised by him; Sydenham embraced careful observation of disease. [D]

His biographer H. R. Fox Bourne wrote that about 1670 Locke began to have a cough that seriously troubled him through the remainder of his life, and that an undated fragment in his hand from those years, titled 'Tussis', was the start of a paper on coughs. His health was already weak by the early 1670s; a letter from Sydenham, probably at the end of 1674, advised him to go to bed early and be very temperate and cautious, and from late 1675 to 1677 he lived in France, mostly at Montpellier, then much visited by invalids. [D]

Lady Masham later wrote that although his travels in France had done his health some good, after his return he was still less able than before to stay long in London without retreating to a neighbouring village 'to recover the prejudice his health received from the smoke of that vast quantity of sea-coal which is burnt in this great city'. From then on he left London as often as he could, and always in the winter months. [D]

Among his medical papers, an account of consumption that Fox Bourne describes as drawn from Sydenham's observation and confirmed by Locke attributes the frequency of consumptions in London to 'a perpetual mist' mixed with the fumes of the city's trades, 'but especially the sulphur and fumes of sea coals, with which the air is repleted; and these being sucked into our lungs ... give an occasion to a cough'. [D]

He left England in the autumn of 1683, when he was under suspicion for his association with Shaftesbury, lived in Holland, and landed at Greenwich on 12 February 1688/9 (Julian). He soon declined a diplomatic mission on the ground of insufficient health, and wrote in April 1689 that he hoped to breathe more easily and be less troubled by his cough. [D]

He found the smoke of London unfavourable to his health, and from the spring of 1691 lived at Oates, in the parish of High Laver, Essex, the home of Sir Francis and Lady Masham (Damaris Cudworth). [D]

On 29 February 1691/2 (Julian; 10 March 1692, Gregorian) he wrote to Philipp van Limborch that since visiting Robert Boyle on his deathbed in December, 'my health has kept me in the country, for I found my lungs could not bear the smoke of the city'. [D]

list.item: Asthma with persistent airflow limitation, type 2 phenotype (J45.40). He has airflow limitation that persists after bronchodilator (FEV1/FVC 0.62, below the lower limit of normal and below 0.70) with a large bronchodilator response. GOLD recognizes COPD in never-smokers from air pollution and solid-fuel smoke, so COPD was considered. The weight of evidence is for asthma: onset in his late thirties, symptoms that vary with season, cold, and smoke, a bronchodilator response of 380 mL, FeNO 41 ppb, eosinophils 0.46 x 10^3/uL, a raised IgE, a normal DLCO, and a CT showing airway disease without emphysema. The persistent limitation most likely reflects decades of under-treated asthma with airway remodeling, worsened by pollution and indoor smoke. Treat as asthma: an inhaled corticosteroid is essential, and a long-acting bronchodilator without one is unsafe. Tuberculosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, heart failure, and bronchiectasis are excluded. [S]

Exposure to air pollution and indoor solid-fuel smoke (Z77.110). Fine particles from coal, wood, and traffic smoke are well-established triggers of asthma symptoms and flares and contribute to lower lung function. Removing indoor solid-fuel smoke is the most effective step within his control; outdoor exposure can be reduced but not removed. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Spirometry this morning (GLI Global race-neutral equations): FEV1 2.11 L (62 percent predicted) and FVC 3.71 L before bronchodilator, FEV1/FVC 0.57; 15 minutes after albuterol 400 mcg, FEV1 2.49 L (+380 mL, 11 percent of predicted) and FVC 4.02 L, FEV1/FVC 0.62 (lower limit of normal 0.67); DLCO 26.4 mL/min/mmHg (predicted 26.9); FeNO 41 ppb; six-minute walk 430 m with lowest saturation 94 percent. CT of the chest today without contrast, with expiratory images: diffuse bronchial wall thickening and mosaic attenuation with air trapping; no emphysema, bronchiectasis, nodules, or interstitial disease. From the first visit: eosinophils 0.46 x 10^3/uL, IgE 186 IU/mL, alpha-1 antitrypsin 131 mg/dL, NT-proBNP 58 pg/mL, interferon-gamma release assay negative (0.02 IU/mL), and a chest X-ray with mild hyperinflation only. Asthma Control Test 13 today. [S]

list.item: Diagnosis: asthma with persistent airflow limitation, type 2 phenotype; not COPD. Record the reasoning, and repeat spirometry after three months of treatment to find his best lung function. [S]

CT was indicated for persistent airflow limitation in a never-smoker and was done today; it shows airway disease without emphysema or bronchiectasis. No further imaging unless new features appear. [S]

Start budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 mcg, two inhalations twice daily and one as needed, no more than 12 a day (GINA track 1, step 4), and stop albuterol. Teach technique with his own device and give a written action plan. If he is not well controlled at three months despite good adherence and technique, add tiotropium 2.5 mcg two inhalations daily; consider a biologic only if he has flares needing oral corticosteroids despite that. [S]
Yes: an eight-week pulmonary rehabilitation program, with a six-minute walk before and after. [S]

Keep the open fires out of use permanently and heat his rooms another way; HEPA air cleaners in the rooms where he spends most time; check the air quality index daily and avoid outdoor exertion and city trips when it is 101 or more; a well-fitted N95 respirator on unavoidable alert days; walk away from main roads. The WHO 1687 guideline values for PM2.5 (5 ug/m3 annual, 15 ug/m3 over 24 hours) are a useful target for his indoor monitor. [S]

Monitoring: Asthma Control Test, technique, adherence, and exposures at every visit; spirometry and FeNO at three months, then every one to two years; home peak flow to set action-plan zones; influenza, COVID-19, and RSV vaccines in the autumn and PCV20 now. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Hartwell-Osei the same day; Mr. Locke agrees with the diagnosis and the plan and asked for a copy of the exposure advice for the household. [S]

Follow-up: Primary care continues with Dr. Hartwell-Osei. I will review the three-month spirometry, and would see him again if he is not controlled on add-on tiotropium or has a flare needing oral corticosteroids. [S]
